transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Well, honestly, it’s been a long time coming, I think. I manage a health clinic—I'm a medical services manager—and, you know, at fifty, you'd think I'd have my workflow completely dialed in by now. I've been doing this kind of work for a while, and I try, I really do. I have my desk set up, I have my schedule blocked out, but... well, what finally pushed me to actually make this appointment and come in today is that I just cannot seem to hold my focus on the things I absolutely have to do to keep the clinic running smoothly. 

For example, I’ll sit down at my computer to start an EPIC quality report, which is a huge part of my job, or I’ll go into one of our weekly clinic metrics meetings with the department heads. And I go in with every intention of tracking the data, paying close attention to the compliance numbers, really being present and engaged. But within... I don't know, just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far away. It’s like I’m physically there, but mentally I'm completely gone, thinking about something completely unrelated. 

I'll catch myself rereading the exact same column of numbers on my screen over and over again without absorbing a single thing, or suddenly I'll "wake up" in a meeting and realize I’ve missed the entire point of the discussion the physicians were just having. And it’s not just once in a while. I’m spending hours on reports that should take thirty minutes just because I have to keep backtracking. It’s incredibly frustrating because I know how important these metrics are for our funding and our patient care, and I just sit there thinking, 'why can't I just pay attention like everyone else in the room?' It’s exhausting, to be honest, just trying to keep my head above water, and I felt like I couldn't keep hiding it or working around it anymore.
Looking back to your childhood and school years, did you struggle with your focus and attention back then as well?

Oh, absolutely. Yes, it goes way, way back. It’s funny you ask that, because I was actually just talking to my sister about this the other day, and we were reminiscing, well, if you can call it that, about how much of a struggle school was for me. I mean, I wasn't failing or anything—I always managed to scrape by because I was smart enough to figure things out at the last minute—but it was never easy. 

Even in elementary school, I vividly remember the comments on my report cards. It was always the same thing, year after year. The teachers would write these little notes, you know, in that neat cursive they all seemed to have, saying things like, "She's very bright, but she's so careless," or "She has so much potential if she would just apply herself and pay attention." I hated those comments. It made me feel like I was doing something wrong on purpose, but I wasn't! I just... my brain wouldn't stay put. 

And the homework... oh, the homework was a nightmare. My poor mother. She practically had to tether herself to me at the kitchen table every single night just to make sure I got it done. If she walked away for five minutes to stir a pot on the stove or answer the phone, I’d be off in my own world, staring at a spot on the wall or playing with my pencil eraser, completely oblivious to the math worksheet sitting right in front of me. She had to constantly redirect me. And that’s if I even brought the homework home in the first place! Half the time, I’d completely lose track of what the assignments even were, or I'd leave the textbook I needed sitting right in my desk at school. I’d get all the way home, sit down, and realize I didn't have the one book I needed to answer the questions. It drove my parents crazy, and honestly, it drove me crazy too, even back then. I just always felt like I was scrambling to keep up with things that seemed so effortless for the other kids. So, yes, it’s definitely not a new problem, it's just... well, it feels like the stakes are so much higher now with my career.
Aside from the frustration with your focus, have you been experiencing a persistent feeling of sadness or a depressed mood?

No, no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling sad or depressed. I mean, I know what that looks like, working in healthcare, you see a lot of depression, and I really don't think that's what's going on with me. It’s not a heavy, dark cloud kind of feeling, you know? I still enjoy my weekends, I love spending time with my family, I like going out to dinner... I don't have that sense of hopelessness or anything like that. 

The primary emotion I feel is just... intense frustration. And maybe a bit of anxiety, but only because I'm constantly worried I'm going to drop the ball at work. Like, if I'm sitting there and I know I have a deadline for a compliance audit, and I just can't get my brain to engage with the spreadsheet, I get so mad at myself. I'll think, "Come on, just do it, it's right in front of you!" But it's not sadness. It's more like being trapped in a car where the engine is running but the transmission won't engage. 

I guess sometimes the frustration can feel a little overwhelming, and maybe someone looking from the outside might mistake that for being down, because I’ll come home from the clinic just totally drained. I'll collapse on the couch and tell my husband I'm exhausted, but it's an exhaustion from fighting my own brain all day, not an exhaustion from life in general, if that makes sense. I still want to do things, I still have goals, I still care about my job—probably too much, honestly, which is why this is bothering me so much. But no, a persistent sadness? No, I definitely wouldn't say I have that. It's really just the focus and the mental drifting that are driving me up a wall.
Do you find yourself worrying excessively about a variety of everyday matters, like health, finances, or family, beyond just your work performance?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I worry about things, sure, because who doesn't? But it's not this constant, overwhelming dread about everything in my life. Like, I don't sit up at night agonizing over our retirement accounts or stressing that my husband is going to get into a car accident on his way to work. I'm pretty practical about that kind of stuff. I check our finances, they look fine, I move on. 

And health-wise, being a clinic manager, you'd think I'd be a massive hypochondriac with all the things I see, but I'm really not. I know what the red flags are, I get my mammograms, I get my blood work done, and unless my doctor tells me something is wrong, I don't give it a second thought. I don't spiral into thinking every headache is a brain tumor, you know? 

Even with my family, my kids are grown and out of the house, and they're doing well. One's an engineer, the other's in grad school, and I'm incredibly proud of them. I might worry a little if they call me sounding stressed, but it's a normal mom worry, not this consuming anxiety. 

It always, always comes back to work. That's where the anxiety lives. It's the fear of dropping the ball because my brain decided to take a vacation during a crucial meeting. Like last Tuesday, I had this moment of sheer panic because I couldn't remember if I had actually submitted the quarterly staffing report, or if I had just dreamed that I submitted it while I was staring blankly at my monitor for twenty minutes. I had to log back in from home at 8 PM just to check, and my heart was pounding the whole time. But that's all tied to my inability to just sit down and focus. If I didn't have this constant battle with my own attention span, I really don't think I'd be an anxious person at all. I'm actually a very organized, capable person by nature... it's just that my brain refuses to cooperate with my own systems! So no, I wouldn't say I have excessive worry about everyday life stuff, just the work things that I know I'm messing up.
